 Roy Erasmus Sr.: Darker mornings are ahead for us
 Published 6:47 am Tuesday, November 17, 2026
 1/2 
 Swipe or click to see more 
 2/2 
 Swipe or click to see more 
 This is what the sunrise times will look like on Dec. 21, the shortest day of the year. Not going back to standard time will make the sun rise later and that's not good, writes columnist Roy Erasmus Sr. 
 (Image courtesy of Roy Erasmus Sr.) 
 Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... 
 For years Canada has been moving the time an hour forward in the spring which is called daylight saving time. Then we move the time an hour back in the fall and this is called Mountain Standard Time here in the NWT.
 Apparently, this practice caused an old Indian chief to say, “Only the government would believe that you could cut a foot off the top of a blanket, sew it to the bottom, and say it’s a longer blanket.” Eschia (take it easy eh!)
 On Nov. 1, the NWT stopped changing the time. We moved the time ahead in the spring, but we did not move our clocks back an hour in November. This means we have remained in daylight saving time.
 That’s good, right? After all, people have been complaining about having to change the time, including me. I’ve been complaining for years. But I’m saying it’s good we have stopped changing the time, but we should not have stayed in daylight savings time. We should have put our clocks back on Nov. 1 and just kept it there. That would be standard time and we have lived all of our lives in standard time except for a couple of months in the summer.
 There are compelling reasons why we should have stayed with standard time, and the biggest reason that we can easily see is that the sun is rising later every day. In fact, on Dec. 21, sunrise in Yellowknife will be at 11:06 am. In 2025, sunrise was at 10:06 am. Can you imagine the sun coming up at 11:06 am? That means it will still be partially dark around 11:15 am in the morning.
 Circadian Rhythm – body’s master clock 
 Let’s look at our “body’s master clock,” which is known as the circadian rhythm. Way back in the day, there were no light bulbs. This meant that people would generally wake up when the sun rose, worked and played until dusk, then went to bed soon after the sun went down. The “body’s master clock” is a group of cells in the brain that regulates most of our bodily functions. The “body’s master clock” is ruled by the 24-hour cycle of sunlight and darkness. 
 As mentioned above, this system is technically known as the circadian rhythm. The way it works is by sunlight. As the sun begins to rise, “the master clock” receives light input directly from the eye and uses that information to synchronize the 24-hour day. So, if the sun now rises an hour later than it used to, our master clocks will be thrown off. It can also throw off the secondary clocks in cells in the heart, gut, muscles, and more.
 It may affect your gut including constipation or diarrhea; it may affect your heart rate and adults are much more likely to suffer a heart attack in the morning than at night. It can also influence your metabolism. People in a study who were exposed only to afternoon sun were less physically active than those exposed to sun in the morning.
 Bad for students 
 Patrick Baylis, associate professor of economics and the Vancouver School of Economics, is quite concerned about students going to school in the dark. He said a study of students in Florida showed that adolescent students having an extra hour of sunlight before school got higher math and reading scores. The analysis said it was “comparable in magnitude to meaningful class-size reductions,”
 Similarly, an article on the American Psychological Association’s website reads, “For decades, psychologists and other researchers have amassed evidence that later school start times can improve adolescents’ health and well-being. Finally, that evidence is translating to broad shifts in policy … But progress was piecemeal until 2014, when the American Academy of Pediatrics
helped draw attention to the cause by publishing a position statement stating that middle schools and high schools should begin no earlier than 8:30 a.m.”
 What we are doing here is going backwards. Today, when school starts at 8:30 a.m., our children’s “master body clocks” are still actually at 7:30 am. Considering this, I believe we can expect school marks to get worse because of this move to remain at daylight saving time. NWT education and graduation levels are bad enough; giving our kids one hour less of daylight in the morning can only make those levels worse.
 Russia and the U.S. already tried it
In 2011, Russia switched to permanent daylight saving time. The government said medical reports showed an increase in morning road accidents after it was made permanent. In 2014, Russian president Vladimir Putin changed it back to standard time after a survey showed over two-thirds of Russians wanted to change it to permanent standard time.
 Apparently, the permanent daylight saving change was popular when it first happened but it created stress and health problems. This was especially true for people living in northern Russia. This may sound familiar, but they already had dark winter mornings and it now remained darker for an hour longer during the winter months.
 Similarly, in 1974, Richard Nixon signed the Emergency Conservation Act to have year-round daylight saving time across the U.S. to conserve oil during the Arab oil embargo. The policy was abandoned within a year because of opposition to dark winter mornings. There was also concern about children travelling to school and adults to work before sunrise; to boot, the energy savings the act was supposed to create did not materialize.
 Putin and Nixon were smart enough to listen to their people who did not like darker mornings. Here in Yellowknife, we have four months where the sun will rise after 9 a.m. Let’s hope our leaders take similar action for permanent standard time and change our clocks back an hour after we live through a winter with an extra hour of darkness each morning.
 If you agree with me that it will be too dark in the morning because of the time change, please tell your MLA to change it back to standard time.
